catalog_quote: L'accent tonique porte en général sur la pénultième sauf lorsque celle-ci comporte une voyelle longue⁵. Dans ce cas, l'accent tonique porte sur la dernière syllabe: fále "maison", tái "mer", 'átu "lancer"; maháki "malade", alága "cuisse", peáu "vague" mais matapā́ "porte", falā́ "argent", fakapṓ "assassiner". L'accent tonique ordinaire ne sera pas noté dans le reste de l'ouvrage; en effet, nous réservons le caractère graphique de l'accent aigu à la notation de l'accent tonique marquant la définitude. [footnote 5] De fait, il est plus exact de dire que l'accent porte toujours sur l'avant-dernière more. Lorsque la voyelle finale est brève, l'avant-dernière more est aussi l'avant-dernière syllabe; mais une voyelle longue étant composée de deux mores, l'accent tonique affecte la première more de la voyelle longue, et c'est donc l'ensemble de la dernière syllabe qui se trouve accentuée. [Livingston 2016 p. 13] In words of three syllables or fewer, the penultimate mora receives primary stress and secondary stress is absent. Thus words ending in [ˈCV.CV] to be stressed on the penultimate syllable and words ending in bimoraic [ˈCV,V] to be stressed on the penultimate mora. [p. 18] East Uvean has predictable stress on the penultimate mora of a word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Dans ce cas, l'accent tonique porte sur la dernière syllabe : fále "maison", tái "mer", 'átu "lancer" ; maháki "malade", alága "cuisse", peáu "vague" mais matapā́ "porte", falā́ "argent", fakapṓ "assassiner". [fn 5:] De fait, il est plus exact de dire que l'accent porte toujours sur l'avant-dernière more. Lorsque la voyelle finale est brève, l'avant-dernière more est aussi l'avant-dernière syllabe ; mais une voyelle longue étant composée de deux mores, l'accent tonique affecte la première more de la voyelle longue, et c'est donc l'ensemble de la dernière syllabe qui se trouve accentuée.
new_statements.translation: Stress generally falls on the penultimate, except when it [the final syllable] contains a long vowel. In that case stress falls on the final syllable: fále 'house', tái 'sea', 'átu 'throw'; maháki 'sick', alága 'thigh', peáu 'wave', but matapā́ 'door', falā́ 'money', fakapṓ 'murder'. [fn 5:] In fact it is more accurate to say that stress always falls on the penultimate mora. When the final vowel is short, the penultimate mora is also the penultimate syllable; but since a long vowel consists of two morae, stress affects the first mora of the long vowel, and so it is the whole final syllable that ends up stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate mora: on the penultimate syllable when the final vowel is short, and on the final syllable when the final vowel is long (a long vowel counting as two morae). Note: the main text says 'sauf lorsque celle-ci comporte une voyelle longue' where 'celle-ci' must refer to the final syllable, since all the counter-examples have long final vowels; footnote 5 makes this explicit. Livingston 2016 (p. 13, p. 17) states the same rule independently: 'East Uvean has predictable stress on the penultimate mora of a word.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Moyse-Faurie 2016 says nothing about secondary stress. Livingston 2016 p. 13: absent in words of three syllables or fewer; in longer words it 'cannot currently be shown to have a fully predictable rule, but tends to fall two morae before the primary stressed unit' (tapu'aki /ˌta.pu.ˈʔa.ki/; fe.ˌtau.ˈʔa.ki).
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose final syllable contains a long vowel are stressed on that final syllable (matapā́ 'porte', falā́ 'argent', fakapṓ 'assassiner') — subsumed by the penultimate-mora formulation in footnote 5. Definitive accent (grammatically conditioned shift to the final vowel, with lengthening and a slight rise in pitch) marks definiteness; incompatible with the non-specific article.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('rôle démarcatif au niveau du mot'); examples are citation forms. At phrase level a separate 'accent de définitude' shifts stress to the final vowel of the last word of a definite noun phrase (§1.3.2, pp. 18-21). Loanwords: closed-syllable French sources get an added final vowel and penultimate stress; open-syllable French sources keep original final stress by a long final vowel (kamiō, sinemā; pp. 28-29).
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the language of Wallis ('Uvea) island as a whole (faka'uvea / wallisien); no dialect specified. Not to be confused with West Uvean (Fagauvea, New Caledonia, glottocode west2517), whose accent Moyse-Faurie treats separately.

sources.note: §1.3.1 (p. 17-18): ordinary stress falls on the penultimate syllable except when the final syllable has a long vowel, in which case it falls on the final syllable; footnote 5: more exactly, stress always falls on the penultimate mora. §1.3.2 (pp. 18-21): a 'definitive accent' (stress shift to the final vowel, with lengthening and slight pitch rise) marks definiteness of the noun phrase. Pp. 28-29: French loans ending in a closed syllable get an added final vowel and penultimate stress; open-syllable French loans keep final stress via a long final vowel (kamiō 'camion').
